# ONS Analysis Standards and Pipelines hub, the Duck Book (quality assurance of code for analysis and research), Warranting Agent-Built Software Distillation

**Source:** Analysis Standards and Pipelines hub, Office for National Statistics, for the UK Government Analysis Function. *Quality assurance of code for analysis and research* ("the Duck Book"), web book, version 2026.1, repository commit fa39f20 (2026-06-09). No individual authors named. Licence: Open Government Licence v3.0; contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0. **Scope:** open. Citations take the form `(book/{file}.md, "Section heading")`.

**Setting, read before projecting.** The Duck Book is written for analysts in UK government who write code to produce statistics, models and research, often as their own developers, inside a profession that already runs a proportionate assurance regime. Its managers' guide argues that a manager need not read the code to trust it, *because* a team has applied agreed practices and supplements code assurance with output checks where it falls short. Its generative AI chapter is about a human coder using an LLM assistant ("vibe coding"), and its first golden rule requires that coder to review every line the LLM wrote. It does not discuss autonomous coding agents, client contracts or production services. This distillation carries both arguments onto agent-built software and keeps the gap between them visible: the manager's argument transfers to the accountable builder only to the extent the harness does what the Duck Book's team does, and the golden rule does not stop applying because an agent wrote the code.

**Applicability gate (Pass G.0): clear yes.** (1) The source asks the axis's own questions: how a person who does not read the code can trust it, what was shown rather than claimed, how tests earn trust, who is responsible for LLM-generated code. (2) Its practices land on every phase, strongest on locking the tests, gating, reviewing and warranting. (3) Its contrarian positions (expected outcomes never copied from the code's output, review only at the end loses its value, unreviewed LLM code is never submitted, offloading design to the model makes the human a reverse-centaur) bear directly on the axis's three reflexes.

**Phase mapping.**

| Phase | Fit | What the source brings |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Specifying the change | Moderate | Documentation as specification written before the code; requirements captured before coding; precise, bounded prompts (centaur) over vague ones; users consulted from the start |
| 2 Triaging risk | Moderate | Proportionate assurance agreed before work starts; external review and dual running for novel, complex, business-critical or high-risk work; sensitive-data rules. It carries no security threat classes |
| 3 Locking the tests | Strong | Expected outcomes created independently, never copied from output; tests before logic; a test per bug; repeatable, deterministic tests; mocks whose calls are asserted |
| 4 Building in the sandbox | Partial | Plausible-but-inaccurate output; no sensitive input to a chatbot; tests isolated from production systems; dependency hygiene. Nothing on agent permissions or isolation |
| 5 Gating deterministically | Strong | All tests pass before every merge; CI that blocks the merge; hooks, linters and formatters; reproducible runs in a clean environment; configuration on record; skipped tests need a plan back |
| 6 Reviewing independently | Strong | Review by someone other than the author; early, small, frequent review; documented outcomes acted on before use; merges blocked without an approved pull request; the author's own review of LLM code first |
| 7 Warranting the change | Strong | The manager's trust argument and its condition; sole responsibility for LLM code; assumptions communicated; a statement of assurance done and still owed; test outcomes recorded with the code version |
| 8 Releasing and operating | Partial | Informative failures and logged errors; comparison with previous results and parallel running against the system being replaced; a test for every bug found; breach handling for leaked secrets |

Triggers addressed: 21 of the seed table's 41 (see the runtime section). No trigger-mismatch flag.

## Warranting Agent-Built Software Relevance

The Duck Book answers the question at the centre of this axis from inside a working assurance regime: how does someone accountable for code trust it without reading it? Its answer is conditional. A manager "should not need an in-depth understanding of the analysis code to trust that it is working correctly" [V], but only because the manager is confident the team took an appropriate approach and applies proportionate assurance, agreed in advance, and where that assurance falls short the manager adds checks on the outputs, such as dual running (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk"). For a builder warranting agent-built software, that turns the warranty into a question about the harness: does it do, demonstrably and on the record, what the Duck Book's team does? Tests whose expected outcomes were set independently of the code, run on every change and recorded against the code version; review by someone other than the author, early and on small changes; configuration and data versions on record so the result can be reproduced; and a written statement of what assurance has been done and what is still owed.

The book's generative AI chapter supplies the other half. It says LLMs produce plausible but inaccurate output by design, that the person who generated code with an LLM is the only one responsible for it, that no LLM code goes to peer review unread by its author, and that the human should direct the model rather than pick up after it (book/generative_ai.md). The first rule is in tension with the axis premise that nobody reads every line. The honest projection is that the Duck Book does not license skipping the author's review; it licenses a *manager* not reading code that a team has assured. Where the harness replaces that team, every gap in it lands back on the accountable builder, who is, in the book's terms, the only person responsible.

## Key Concepts for Warranting Agent-Built Software

1. <!-- concept: proportionate-assurance --> **Proportionate assurance, agreed before the work starts.** Government advocates "the right quality assurance procedures for the right analysis" [V] (book/principles.md, "Assured"). Following the Aqua book [BT], assurance scales with complexity and risk; managers decide with the team which practices a piece of work needs and, when possible, define the target assurance level before starting (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk"). External review is recommended for novel or complex techniques, where comparison with other analyses cannot challenge the results, or for business-critical work, and dual running should be considered "particularly for high risk analysis" [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Peer review"; book/principles.md, "Assured"). For the harness: the change's assurance level is set at triage, not discovered at sign-off.

2. <!-- concept: trust-without-reading-the-code --> **Trust without reading the code, and its condition.** The manager need not understand the code in depth but must be confident in the team's approach and its proportionate assurance; where code assurance does not meet the target, "for example where there is limited time or skill" [V], it is supplemented with in-depth assurance of outputs, such as dual running with an independent system and consistency checks across output data [AP] (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk"). This is the source's warrant for an accountable builder who reads the warranty pack rather than the diff, and its condition is that the pack shows the practices were done.

3. <!-- concept: llm-golden-rules --> **The three golden rules for LLM-generated code.** Never use or submit LLM code to peer review without first reviewing it yourself; "The only person responsible for the code you generated with an LLM is you." [V]; never enter sensitive information into a chatbot (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace"). Responsibility does not pass to the model or the harness.

4. <!-- concept: plausible-but-inaccurate --> **Plausible but inaccurate is the design, not the failure.** LLMs "can and regularly do generate **plausible but inaccurate** statements" [V]; the book, citing prior work [BT], calls this "mathematically inevitable" [V], and says "Outputs that 'look right' are all that the models are trained to produce." [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace"). An agent's confident report of success is the kind of output the model is built to produce, so it is a claim to check, not evidence.

5. <!-- concept: centaur-and-reverse-centaur --> **Centaur and reverse-centaur.** Borrowing the framing [BT], the book separates a human assisted by a machine from a human who assists a machine and is stripped of agency (book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs"). Its worked example: a vague prompt that offloaded the thinking returned 225 lines, five functions and a class holding only attributes, "practically the size of an entire pull request" [V] to review; a precise prompt returned one 46-line function [AE]. A builder who specifies loosely becomes the agent's full-time reviewer.

6. <!-- concept: reproducibility-first --> **Reproducibility first.** "Reproducibility is the only thing that you can guarantee in your analysis." [V] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible"). Scripts run end to end in a clean environment, outputs are disposable, and configuration files are passed as arguments so the configuration behind each output is on record (book/project_structure.md, "Run scripts from end to end to ensure your code is executed reproducibly"; "Check that outputs are disposable"; book/configuration.md, "Use configuration files as arguments"). A result nobody can regenerate from recorded code, data and configuration has not been shown.

7. <!-- concept: independent-expected-outcomes --> **Expected outcomes set independently of the code.** "You must not copy the output from running your code to create your expected test outcomes." [V], because that assumes the code already works (book/testing_code.md, "Minimise your test data"). Test data is minimal, fake, static and readable, and built to reflect intended behaviour (book/testing_code.md, "Minimise your test data"). This is the source's sharpest rule against tests that an agent fits to its own output.

8. <!-- concept: repeatable-recorded-tests --> **Repeatable tests, run on every change, outcomes recorded.** Tests are independent and deterministic where possible, so "the only reason for a test to fail should be that the code being tested is incorrect" [V] (book/testing_code.md, "Write repeatable tests"); all tests run against each change; outcomes are recorded with the code version, most simply through CI (book/testing_code.md, "Run all tests against each change to your code"; "Record the outcomes of your tests"). "Automating the running of unit tests is especially important to establish trust in your pipeline or package, by ensuring that all unit tests pass before every merge." [V] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Motivation").

9. <!-- concept: tests-before-logic --> **Tests before logic, and a test for every bug.** "The best practice for testing code is to use test-driven development (TDD)." [V]: the desired outcome is known in advance, so the test comes first (book/testing_code.md, "Write tests before writing logic"). Each bug found gets a test, which "increases the coverage of your tests in a proportionate way" [V] (book/testing_code.md, "Write tests to assure that bugs are fixed"). The book flags its own TDD section as framed more like training, likely to change once dedicated training exists [AP] (book/testing_code.md, "Write tests before writing logic").

10. <!-- concept: peer-review-early-and-small --> **Peer review by someone other than the author, early and on small changes.** Peer review is "a quality assurance activity where a developer, other than the code's author, views and tests the usage of a piece of code" [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Peer review"). Reviewers ask whether they understand the code, whether testing is proportionate to the risk, and whether they can reproduce the claimed outputs (book/peer_review.md, "Focus reviews on code quality"); feedback is acted on or justified before use and recorded with the code version (book/peer_review.md, "Document review feedback and outcomes"); merges to `main` can be blocked "without an approved Pull Request to enforce peer review" [V] (book/version_control.md, "Use pull requests for reviewing changes").

11. <!-- concept: auditable-change-record --> **The auditable change record.** Auditable work can answer "Who made each decision?", "When was this decision made?" and "What evidence was this decision based on?" [V] (book/principles.md, "Auditable"). Version control records what changed, when, why and by whom, and each change is linked to a reason (book/version_control.md, "Keep an audit trail of changes"; book/managers_guide.md, "How will you keep track of changes to the code and why they were made?"). For the harness this is the change's ledger.

12. <!-- concept: assurance-statement-to-users --> **Telling users what was assured and what was not.** Assumptions are recorded close to the code, and "You must communicate these to users when releasing results from the analysis." [V] (book/managers_guide.md, "What assumptions does the analysis make?"). Desk instructions say what quality assurance "has been carried out and what further quality assurance of outputs is required" [V] (book/project_documentation.md, "User desk instructions"); guarantees of assurance are published with the report (book/principles.md, "Assured"). Skipped tests need "a plan for going back to add them" [V] (book/testing_code.md, "In a time crunch? The risks to skipping tests"). This is the source's shape for a warranty pack that is honest about what remains.

## Questions to Ask During Warranting Agent-Built Software

### Phase 1: Specifying the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness written down | Is there a written description of what this change is expected to do, written before the code, that a test can be built from? | book/code_documentation.md, "Docstrings"; book/testing_code.md, "Write tests before writing logic" |
| Precise direction | Did the prompt state the data, the behaviour and the thresholds, or did it hand the agent the design and ask it to meet *quality standards*? | book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs" |
| Scope held down | Were requirements captured before coding, and does the change carry cases nobody asked for? | book/readable_code.md, "Keep it simple" |
| Users in view | Who will use the result, and were they consulted at the start and kept in view? | book/managers_guide.md, "Why have you chosen to do the analysis this way?" |

### Phase 2: Triaging risk

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Target level | What assurance level did we agree for this change, and was it set before the agent started? | book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk" |
| Escalation | Is the change novel, complex, business critical, or impossible to check against another result? If so, where is the external review? | book/peer_review.md, "Peer review" |
| High risk | For a high-risk change, is anything running it a second way (an independent system, consistency checks across outputs)? | book/principles.md, "Assured"; book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk" |
| Sensitive material | Did any credential, personal data or real configuration reach the agent's prompt, the repository or its history? | book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace"; book/version_control.md, "Exclude sensitive information from version control" |

### Phase 3: Locking the tests

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Independent expectations | Where did each expected value come from: the intended behaviour, or a run of the new code? | book/testing_code.md, "Minimise your test data" |
| Order | Were the tests written before the logic, or by the same session after it? | book/testing_code.md, "Write tests before writing logic" |
| Test edits | When a test changed, did the intended behaviour change in the spec, or did the expectation move to match the code? | book/testing_code.md, "Run all tests against each change to your code"; "Minimise your test data" |
| Edge cases | Do the tests cover missing data, zeroes, negatives, wrong types and invalid inputs, and does the testing match the risk? | book/managers_guide.md, "How have you tested the code?"; book/peer_review.md, "Is the required functionality tested sufficiently?" |
| Mocks | Does each mocked test assert the mock was called, so a broken mock cannot let a real call through while the test passes? | book/testing_code.md, "Isolate code tests from external systems" |
| Bugs | Does every bug fixed in this change come with a test that would have caught it? | book/testing_code.md, "Write tests to assure that bugs are fixed" |

### Phase 4: Building in the sandbox

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Claims | Is the agent's report of success backed by anything other than output that looks right? | book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace" |
| External systems | Can the agent's test runs touch a production database or a paid API? | book/testing_code.md, "Isolate code tests from external systems" |
| Dependencies | Is a new package needed, or does an existing one already in use do the job? Is it new or little used, and so less likely to be tested? | book/readable_code.md, "Keep it simple"; book/testing_code.md, "Test that new logic is correct using unit tests" |
| Size | Is the change far larger than the request, the sign of a prompt that offloaded the design? | book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs" |

### Phase 5: Gating deterministically

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Merge gate | Does CI run every test on every change and block the merge on failure? | book/continuous_integration.md, "Motivation"; "Configure GitHub actions to automate tests" |
| Determinism | Could this test fail for any reason other than wrong code (shared state, order, unseeded randomness)? | book/testing_code.md, "Write repeatable tests" |
| Reproduction | Does the change run end to end in a clean environment, on a machine other than the one that built it, and give the same results? | book/project_structure.md, "Run scripts from end to end to ensure your code is executed reproducibly"; book/managers_guide.md, "What are the dependencies?" |
| Configuration | Is the configuration behind this result on record, or was behaviour switched by editing or commenting out code? | book/configuration.md, "Use configuration files as arguments"; book/code_documentation.md, "Comments" |
| Skipped gates | If a test was set aside, where is the plan to add it back? | book/testing_code.md, "In a time crunch? The risks to skipping tests" |

### Phase 6: Reviewing independently

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Independence | Was this reviewed by someone (or something) other than its author? | book/peer_review.md, "Peer review" |
| Timing | Is review happening on small changes as they land, or on the finished whole? | book/peer_review.md, "Review separately when necessary" |
| Reviewer questions | Can the reviewer explain what the code does, judge whether testing is proportionate, and regenerate the claimed outputs? | book/peer_review.md, "Focus reviews on code quality" |
| Outcomes | Is each review comment answered (acted on or justified) and recorded against the version reviewed, before the change is used? | book/peer_review.md, "Document review feedback and outcomes" |
| Author's pass | Before the reviewer saw it, did the accountable human review the LLM-written code at all? | book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace" |

### Phase 7: Warranting the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Basis for trust | Am I signing because the pack shows the agreed practices were done, or because I trust the agent? | book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk" |
| Shortfall | Where code assurance fell short of the target, what output checks made up the difference? | book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk" |
| Responsibility | Who is responsible for this code once the session ends, and could they explain it? | book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace"; book/managers_guide.md, "How is the analysis documented?" |
| Disclosure | Does the pack state the assumptions, the assurance done, and the assurance still owed? | book/managers_guide.md, "What assumptions does the analysis make?"; book/project_documentation.md, "User desk instructions" |
| Run record | Are the test outcomes recorded against this code version, or only reported? | book/testing_code.md, "Record the outcomes of your tests" |

### Phase 8: Releasing and operating

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Replacement | If this replaces an existing system, have the two run in parallel and their differences been explained? | book/managers_guide.md, "How does the analysis result differ from the previous analysis?" |
| Failure | When it fails, does it fail with a message another team could act on, and are errors logged in production? | book/managers_guide.md, "What happens when the analysis fails to run?" |
| Recurrence | Has each error found after release become a test? | book/managers_guide.md, "How have you tested the code?"; book/testing_code.md, "Write tests to assure that bugs are fixed" |
| Leaks | If a secret or personal data reached the repository, has access been closed, history rewritten and the credential changed? | book/version_control.md, "Handle data breaches via Git" |

## What to Look For

| Signal | Diagnosis | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| A test's expected values match the current output to the last decimal, and nobody can say where they came from | Expected outcomes copied from the code's own output, which assumes the code already works (book/testing_code.md, "Minimise your test data") | Rebuild the expectations from the intended behaviour, on minimal hand-written data, and rerun |
| A failing test was "fixed" by editing its expected value, with no change to the spec | The expectation moved to match the code; the source's allowance for updating tests covers changed *functionality* (book/testing_code.md, "Run all tests against each change to your code") | Ask which spec change required the new expectation; if none, revert the test and fix the code |
| The agent's change is several times the size of the request | A vague prompt that offloaded the design; the builder is about to become the reviewer of code the model designed (book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs") | Re-specify the data, behaviour and limits and regenerate, rather than review the oversized change |
| Review starts only when the whole feature is finished | End-only review, which significantly reduces review's benefit and makes retrofitting tests and documentation costly (book/peer_review.md, "Review separately when necessary") | Split the work into small changes reviewed as they land |
| The pack says "tests pass" and links no CI run for this version | A claim, not a record; the source records test outcomes with the code version (book/testing_code.md, "Record the outcomes of your tests") | Return the pack for the run record |
| A result differs between two runs or two machines | The change is not reproducible: hidden state, unrecorded dependencies, or machine-specific configuration (book/project_structure.md; book/managers_guide.md, "What are the dependencies?") | Run end to end in a clean environment with recorded dependencies and configuration until results match |
| The builder signs because reading the diff would take too long, and the pack is thin | The manager's argument used without its condition (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk") | Name the shortfall and add output assurance (a second run by an independent route, consistency checks) or hold the sign-off |
| A credential appears in the agent's prompt, a config file or a commit | A breach of the third golden rule or of version-control hygiene; deleting the file and committing is not enough (book/generative_ai.md; book/version_control.md, "Handle data breaches via Git") | Restrict access, rewrite history, change the credential, report to the data owner |

## When to Use This Reference

Reach for this source when:

- The question is how an accountable person can trust code they did not read, and what must be true of the team or harness for that trust to hold.
- The tests are the warranty and the question is whether they earn it: where expectations came from, whether they are repeatable, whether they run on every change and whether the runs are recorded.
- The work is data processing, analysis, modelling or a pipeline, where reproducing the same output from the same code, data and configuration is the core check.
- A builder is leaning on an LLM and needs the responsibility rule stated plainly, or a vague prompt has produced a change too big to review.
- The pack needs a disclosure section: assumptions, assurance done, assurance still owed.

Reach elsewhere for security requirements and threat classes (`owasp-asvs-5-0`, `owasp-llm-top10-2026`, `nist-ssdf-1-1`, `nist-sp-800-218a`), for agent permissions and sandboxing (`openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai`, `owasp-agentic-top10-2026`, `owasp-agentic-threats-mitigations`), for measured evidence on agents' tests or productivity (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`, `jimenez-swe-bench`, `becker-metr-ai-developer-productivity-2025`, `he-cursor-velocity-complexity-2025`), and for the formal roles of commissioner, assurer and approver (`uk-aqua-book-2025`). This source states practice and gives worked examples; it carries little measured evidence of its own.

## Worked Example

A two-person firm uses coding agents to build a data pipeline that calculates monthly commission payments for a client's sales staff. The agent reports the change done, all tests green. The accountable builder has not read the 900-line diff and does not plan to.

**The warrant the builder is reaching for.** The Duck Book's managers' guide supports signing without reading the code, on a condition:

> A manager "should not need an in-depth understanding of the analysis code to trust that it is working correctly" [V]

(book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk"). The guide places the trust in the team's approach and its proportionate assurance, agreed before work starts. So the builder's question shifts from *is the code right?* to *does the pack show the agreed practices were done?* Commission payments are money owed to people, so at triage the builder sets the target high and plans a second run by an independent route as the guide's supplement where code assurance falls short (Concept 1, Concept 2).

**The tests.** The reviewer agent, working from a fresh context, opens the test file. The expected commission figures match the pipeline's current output to the penny, and the session log shows the agent ran the pipeline and pasted the results in. The Duck Book's rule:

> "You must create your test data independently, ensuring that it reflects how you want your code to work, rather than how it currently works." [V]

(book/testing_code.md, "Minimise your test data"). The tests are asserted, not demonstrated: they prove the code agrees with itself. The builder writes six rows of fake sales by hand, covering a zero sale, a refund (a negative), a missing region and a rep who crosses a tier threshold, and works the expected commission from the client's written rules (Concept 7; book/managers_guide.md, "How have you tested the code?"). Two fail: the refund raises commission instead of lowering it.

**The LLM rule.** The builder is tempted to have the agent fix the refund case and ship. The golden rules stand in the way of shipping on the agent's word: the author reviews LLM code before peer review, and "The only person responsible for the code you generated with an LLM is you." [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace"). The builder cannot read 900 lines, so the response is to make the change smaller: the commission calculation is split out as one function, specified precisely (inputs, the refund rule, the tier thresholds), regenerated, and read in full, about 50 lines. The rest of the pipeline (loading, formatting) rides on the tests and the second run (Concept 5).

**The gate and the pack.** CI runs every test on the change and blocks the merge until they pass, and the run is recorded against the commit (Concept 8). The pipeline is run against last month's data and compared with the client's existing spreadsheet calculation; three differences are traced, two to the old spreadsheet's rounding and one to a missing region in the new code, which gets a test (book/managers_guide.md, "How does the analysis result differ from the previous analysis?"; Concept 9). The warranty pack states the assumptions (how refunds and tier crossings are treated), the assurance done, and the assurance still owed: the reporting module was not independently reviewed this round, with a date to do it (Concept 12). The builder signs the pack, having read it, and has read the 50 lines that move money.

## Anti-patterns This Reference Helps Avoid

- **Self-confirming tests.** Signal: expected values match current output exactly and have no recorded origin. Diagnosis: expectations copied from the code's output (book/testing_code.md, "Minimise your test data"). Follow-up: rebuild expectations from the specification on minimal hand-written data.
- **The manager's argument without its condition.** Signal: the builder skips the diff and the pack has no recorded test runs, no review record and no output checks. Diagnosis: trust placed in the agent, where the source places it in the team's practices (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk"). Follow-up: list which agreed practices the pack evidences and add output assurance for the rest, or hold.
- **Responsibility handed to the tool.** Signal: *the agent wrote it* offered as an answer to *who stands behind this?* Diagnosis: the second golden rule says the person who generated the code is the only one responsible (book/generative_ai.md). Follow-up: name the human, and confirm they can explain the parts that matter.
- **Reverse-centaur review.** Signal: the builder spends the day reviewing a large change the agent designed from a one-line prompt. Diagnosis: offloading the design turns the human into the model's reviewer (book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs"; "Vibe check failed - The risks of vibe coding"). Follow-up: specify precisely and regenerate small.
- **End-only review.** Signal: the reviewer agent runs once, on the finished branch. Diagnosis: late review loses much of its benefit (book/peer_review.md, "Review separately when necessary"). Follow-up: review each small change as it lands.
- **Success taken as reproducibility.** Signal: *it ran fine on my machine.* Diagnosis: one run in one environment shows nothing about the next (book/principles.md, "Reproducible"; book/project_structure.md). Follow-up: clean-environment run with recorded dependencies, data version and configuration.
- **Silent shortfall.** Signal: tests were skipped for a deadline and the pack does not say so. Diagnosis: technical debt may be necessary for short deadlines but needs time set aside, and skipped tests need a plan to return (book/managers_guide.md; book/testing_code.md, "In a time crunch? The risks to skipping tests"). Follow-up: record the shortfall and the plan in the pack.
- **Access control as the security story.** Signal: *the repo is private, so the key in it is fine.* Diagnosis: access control does not replace good practice, and deleting a leaked file is not enough (book/version_control.md, "Control access to code only when essential"; "Handle data breaches via Git"). Follow-up: rewrite history and change the credential.

## Integration with Other References

| Reference | Relationship |
|---|---|
| `uk-aqua-book-2025` | Parent guidance. The Duck Book takes proportionality from it [BT], and it in turn points to the Duck Book for code assurance and requires the analyst to follow it proportionately while the assurer reviews accordingly. The Aqua book supplies the formal roles (commissioner, analyst, assurer, approver), the independence requirement and formal sign-off once appropriate assurance is confirmed; the Duck Book supplies the code practices the assurer checks. Combine for Phases 2, 6 and 7. See the named tension on review independence below |
| `egashira-testsuitebench-2026` | The Duck Book states the rule (expected outcomes set independently, reflecting intended behaviour); this source measures how far agent-written test suites from specifications fall short of catching seeded faults. Use together at Phase 3: the rule says what the tests must be, the benchmark says why an agent's own suite cannot be assumed to be it |
| `jimenez-swe-bench` | Both judge a change by tests run against it rather than by the author's report. SWE-bench scores agent patches only by running tests associated with the task, which the patch's author did not write; the Duck Book's copy-output warning names the failure that rule guards against |
| `cucumber-bdd-gherkin` | The Duck Book names behaviour-driven development as an extension of TDD focused on user needs [BT]; this source carries that practice in full, with examples as executable specifications written before the code. Use it for Phase 1 where the Duck Book only says to write the test first |
| `microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook` | Agrees on small changes, peer review of every change, TDD and automated style checks, and on tolerating repetition in test code. The playbook carries the engineering-team detail (PR size, reviewer guidance); the Duck Book carries the assurance framing (proportion, reproducibility, disclosure to users) |
| `openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai` | Agrees that humans stay responsible for what AI produces and that human review is needed where failures matter; it carries the agent-specific controls the Duck Book lacks (sandboxing, gates enforced outside the AI, independent verifiers, durable checks). The Duck Book's golden rules are the human-coder version; this source is the agent-harness version |
| `why-language-models-hallucinate-kalai` | Named disagreement on whether hallucination is inevitable (below). Both agree an LLM's confident output is no evidence of correctness |
| `becker-metr-ai-developer-productivity-2025` | The Duck Book cites, borrowed-through, a study finding experienced programmers slower with AI while believing they were faster; this source reports the same finding at first hand, with its conditions. Cite the primary for the numbers |
| `dora-ai-assisted-swdev-2025` | The Duck Book's small, frequent commits and small reviewed changes match DORA's finding that working in small batches amplifies AI's benefit to product performance; DORA supplies the measurement, the Duck Book the practice |
| `he-cursor-velocity-complexity-2025` | The Duck Book asserts that skipping good practice creates technical debt that slows later development; this source measures a persistent rise in warnings and complexity after agent adoption, which its models link to later velocity slowdown. Use together at Phase 8 |

**Named tensions and disagreements.**

- *Hallucination: inevitable, or a product of incentives.* The Duck Book, citing a paper it does not name [BT], says LLM inaccuracy is "mathematically inevitable" [V] and a feature, since models are trained only to produce output that looks right (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace"). `why-language-models-hallucinate-kalai` holds that hallucinations are inevitable only for base models, that a system can avoid them by abstaining, and that they persist because evaluations reward guessing over abstaining. For the harness the practical upshot is the same (check every claim), but the two disagree on whether a better-built system could stop guessing.
- *Review independence: pair programming or an independent assurer.* The Duck Book strongly recommends pair programming as the most timely review method, with the reviewer working alongside the author (book/peer_review.md, "Give timely feedback"; "Review through pair programming"). `uk-aqua-book-2025` says the assurer and the analyst shall be independent, while allowing the analyst to assure as long as there is also formal independent assurance. A tension rather than a contradiction: the Duck Book also recommends external review for high-risk work. For the harness, a reviewer agent that pairs with the builder session counts as the Duck Book's review, not as the Aqua book's independent assurance.

## Citation and Source-Integrity Notes

**Borrowed-through gaps.** The Duck Book takes proportionality from the Aqua book, held in this corpus as `uk-aqua-book-2025` (the deep reference does not say which edition the Duck Book links). Its generative AI chapter cites studies for its claims on hallucination, productivity, learning, wellbeing and security, and borrows the centaur and reverse-centaur framing; all are [BT] here. One productivity study it cites reports the finding held first-hand as `becker-metr-ai-developer-productivity-2025`; the paper it cites for hallucination's inevitability is unnamed in the deep reference and is not identified with any source in this corpus. Its review chapter borrows a feedback model and a published case study, and its managers' guide links published DevOps research as evidence that good practice pays; none is held here.

**Named limits of the source.** Written for analysis and research code in UK government, by and for analysts who often write their own code, inside an existing assurance regime; it does not address client contracts, production services at scale, security threat modelling, or autonomous agents with tools and permissions. Its generative AI chapter is marked a work in progress and treats LLMs as assistants to a human coder. The managers' guide and glossary carry draft banners, and the guide asks for case studies on deciding the level of assurance. The checklists the guide and the review chapter point to have been removed pending an update. SQL testing is out of its scope. It is a living document at version 2026.1; a later version is a re-projection trigger.

**Evidence-marker continuity.** Every quotation marked `[V]` is copied from a `[V]` passage in the deep reference, which passed Pass I on 2026-10-15. The three blockquotes in the worked example and Concept 3 are Pass D key passages or `[V]` admonitions in the deep reference. The managers' guide passage in the worked example is quoted as the deep reference carries it, a fragment introduced by the distillation's own words "A manager", outside the quotation marks. The centaur example's counts (225 and 46 lines) are `[V]` figures in the deep reference's statistics table, carried here as `[AE]` because they describe one worked example. The studies the generative AI chapter cites are `[BT]` in the deep reference and stay `[BT]` here.

## Runtime triggers this source addresses

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| The agent is asked to "build X like Y" with no statement of what must not change | Capture requirements before writing code; keep it simple; the documentation as a specification of what the code is expected to do (book/readable_code.md, "Keep it simple"; book/code_documentation.md, "Docstrings") (Concept 5) | Write down what the change must do and what it must leave alone before the agent starts; the agent only meets requirements it was given. |
| Nobody can say who will use the change or what they will do with it | Consult users at the beginning and throughout (book/managers_guide.md, "Why have you chosen to do the analysis this way?") | Name the user and what they will do with the result before the build; without that, no test can say whether the change is right. |
| The spec is long and the change is large | Small, frequent changes are what separate review works on; commit small changes often (book/peer_review.md, "Review separately when necessary"; book/continuous_integration.md, "Commit small changes often") (Concept 10) | Slice it so each piece can be reviewed and tested as it lands; one big change gets one late review. |
| The builder says "the agent will figure out the details" | Centaur and reverse-centaur: vague prompts that offload the thinking produce oversized output the human must then review (book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs") (Concept 5) | Every detail the agent figures out is one you will review afterwards; decide the design, let the agent type it. |
| The change is business-critical, or complex enough that nobody can predict its effects | Proportionate assurance; external review for novel, complex or business-critical work; dual running for high risk (book/principles.md, "Assured"; book/peer_review.md, "Peer review"; book/managers_guide.md) (Concept 1) | Set the assurance level now: this one gets an outside review and a second run by an independent route before it ships. |
| The tests were written by the same agent session after the code | Tests before logic; expected outcomes created independently of the code, never copied from its output (book/testing_code.md, "Write tests before writing logic"; "Minimise your test data") (Concepts 7, 9) | Treat these tests as the code agreeing with itself; check where each expected value came from before counting them. |
| The agent proposes changing a test so the build goes green | Expected outcomes reflect how the code should work, not how it currently works; failing tests after a functionality change are a reminder to update tests and documentation (book/testing_code.md, "Minimise your test data"; "Run all tests against each change to your code") (Concept 7) | Ask which spec change requires the new expectation. If there is none, the test stays and the code changes. |
| The suite takes minutes, so it runs rarely | Run all tests against each change; automate it in CI so all unit tests pass before every merge (book/testing_code.md; book/continuous_integration.md, "Motivation") (Concept 8) | A test that does not run on this change is not evidence for this change; run them all in CI on every push. |
| The agent adds a dependency nobody asked for | Use existing packages and stick to one of several equivalents; new or little-used packages are less likely to be thoroughly tested; record dependency versions (book/readable_code.md, "Keep it simple"; book/testing_code.md, "Test that new logic is correct using unit tests"; book/managers_guide.md, "What are the dependencies?") | Ask what it adds that the packages already in use don't, and whether anyone has tested it; if it stays, pin and record it. |
| The agent runs for an hour unattended and reports success | LLMs produce plausible but inaccurate output by design; output that looks right is all they are trained to produce (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace") (Concept 4) | A report of success is what the model is built to produce whether or not it succeeded; look for the run record. |
| "It worked first time", or a flaky check passed on retry | Repeatable, deterministic tests where the only reason to fail is wrong code; reproducibility as the one guarantee (book/testing_code.md, "Write repeatable tests"; book/principles.md, "Reproducible") (Concepts 6, 8) | One pass shows it can pass; a flaky test shows the gate can't be trusted. Fix the flakiness before counting the pass. |
| A gate was skipped "just this once" | Skipping tests needs a plan for going back; technical debt may be necessary for deadlines but needs time set aside (book/testing_code.md, "In a time crunch? The risks to skipping tests"; book/managers_guide.md) (Concept 12) | If it's skipped, it goes in the pack with the date it will be done; a silent skip is a false warranty. |
| Lint and type errors are suppressed rather than fixed | Automate style checks with linters and formatters, and use Git hooks to stop failing commits (book/readable_code.md, "Automate style checks"; book/continuous_integration.md, "Use Git hooks to encourage good practice"; "Linters and formatters") | The linter is a gate, so a suppression switches part of it off; list each one for review (treating suppressions as findings is a harness rule, not the source's). |
| The same session that wrote the code reviews it | Peer review is done by a developer other than the code's author (book/peer_review.md, "Peer review") (Concept 10) | The author can't be its own reviewer; route it to a reviewer outside the writing session. |
| The reviewer's findings are long and nobody sorts them | Each piece of feedback is acted on or justified before the analysis is used, and the outcome is recorded with the code version (book/peer_review.md, "Document review feedback and outcomes") | Every finding gets an answer, fixed or argued, on the record, before the change is used. |
| The builder approves because reading the diff is too slow | A manager need not read the code to trust it, if the team's approach and proportionate assurance are sound; shortfalls are made up with output checks (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk") (Concept 2) | Not reading the diff is fine only if the pack shows the practices were done; if it doesn't, add an output check or hold. |
| The pack says "all tests pass" with no run record | Record test outcomes with the code version, most simply through CI (book/testing_code.md, "Record the outcomes of your tests") (Concept 8) | No run record, no pass; send the pack back for the CI run on this commit. |
| The client wants it today and the review is still open | Skipping tests risks hiding problems that grow harder to fix; where assurance falls short for lack of time, supplement with output checks (book/testing_code.md, "In a time crunch? The risks to skipping tests"; book/managers_guide.md) (Concepts 2, 12) | Say what is not yet checked and what that risks; if it ships, the pack says so and names the output check standing in. |
| Nobody could explain how this part works if the agent were unavailable | The person who generated code with an LLM is the only one responsible for it; documentation is essential for business continuity; more than one developer for sustainability (book/generative_ai.md; book/managers_guide.md, "How is the analysis documented?"; "Why have you chosen to do the analysis this way?") (Concept 3) | Before signing, name the human who answers for this part and check they can explain it; the agent can't be held responsible. |
| The builder signs because the last ten went fine | The book cites a study in which experienced programmers using AI were slower yet believed they were faster [BT] (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe check failed - The risks of vibe coding"); reproducibility, not track record, is what can be guaranteed (book/principles.md, "Reproducible") | Ten good runs say how it felt; this change's run record says what happened. Sign on the record. |
| Something went wrong after release | Each identified error gets a test; errors are logged in production with informative messages (book/managers_guide.md, "How have you tested the code?"; "What happens when the analysis fails to run?"; book/testing_code.md, "Write tests to assure that bugs are fixed") (Concept 9) | Write the test that would have caught it before writing the fix, so this bug can't come back unseen. |

## Trigger extensions surfaced by this source

| Trigger (proposed) | Phase | Content from this source | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|---|
| A test's expected values were produced by running the new code (pasted output, generated snapshots) | Phase 3 | "You must not copy the output from running your code to create your expected test outcomes." [V] (book/testing_code.md, "Minimise your test data") | These expectations prove the code agrees with itself; rebuild them from the intended behaviour. |
| A mocked test never asserts that the mock was called | Phase 3 | A broken mock can let a real request run while tests still pass; assert the mock was called (book/testing_code.md, "Isolate code tests from external systems") | Add the assertion that the mock was used, or the test may be passing against the real thing. |
| A credential, personal data or real configuration appears in the agent's prompt, a config file or a commit | Phase 2, Phase 4 | Third golden rule; credentials in environment variables; never in version control; deleting and committing is not sufficient (book/generative_ai.md; book/configuration.md, "Configure secrets as environment variables"; book/version_control.md, "Handle data breaches via Git") | Treat it as exposed: close access, rewrite history, change the credential, tell the data owner. |
| The agent's change is several times larger than the request | Phase 1, Phase 4 | The reverse-centaur example: a vague prompt returned "practically the size of an entire pull request" [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs") | Don't review it; re-specify precisely and regenerate small. |
| The same change gives different results on two runs or two machines | Phase 5 | Run end to end in a clean environment; code not dependent on a specific computer; reproducible outcomes across runs and systems (book/project_structure.md; book/managers_guide.md, "What are the dependencies?") | Until it reproduces, no result from it is evidence; find the hidden state or unrecorded dependency. |
| Behaviour is switched by commenting code in or out, or by editing parameters inside the code | Phase 5 | Comment-toggling is highly discouraged; configuration files record which configuration produced each output (book/code_documentation.md, "Comments"; book/configuration.md, "Use configuration files as arguments") | Move the switch into recorded configuration so the pack can say which settings produced the result. |
| The pack states no assumptions and no assurance still owed | Phase 7 | Assumptions must be communicated to users with the results; desk instructions state assurance done and still required (book/managers_guide.md, "What assumptions does the analysis make?"; book/project_documentation.md, "User desk instructions") | A pack that claims everything was checked is less credible than one that says what wasn't. Add both lists. |
| A change reached the main branch without an approved pull request | Phase 6 | Prevent merges onto `main` "without an approved Pull Request to enforce peer review" [V] (book/version_control.md, "Use pull requests for reviewing changes") | Make approval a branch rule the agent can't bypass, then review what got through. |
| A system is being replaced and the new one was not run alongside the old | Phase 8 | Running replacement and legacy in parallel identifies differences and improvements (book/managers_guide.md, "How does the analysis result differ from the previous analysis?") | Run both on the same inputs and explain every difference before cutting over. |
